newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Blair tiptoes around problem of monarchy's future.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Blair tiptoes around problem of monarchy's future.

text.p: Tony Blair has vowed to establish mini-parliaments in Wales and Scotland. Lords whose titles are hereditary will be no longer be able to vote in the upper house of parliament if Labour wins the May 1 election.

Despite these major reforms, Britain's opposition leader has tiptoed around a problem of far greater interest to voters, and of huge importance to the unwritten British constitution -- the role of the monarchy.

The royal family under Queen Elizabeth became a laughing stock in the 1990s because of the exploits of its most famous younger members -- Prince Charles and his now-divorced wife, Diana, and Sarah, Duchess of York.

Their misdemeanours inside and outside the bedroom were embarrassing enough without the realisation that Charles is heir to the throne and therefore the future head of state of Britain and a clutch of former colonies including Canada and Australia.

The British public has grown increasingly disenchanted with the royals. An opinion poll this year showed 34 percent thought the royal family should be scrapped. A 1996 poll showed only one in three believed Britain would be worse off without a monarchy.

But in the Houses of Parliament, the overwhelming mood remains one of deference and quiet support. That is to be expected from the ruling Conservatives, regarded as being part of the British "establishment" that has the queen at its head.

One government minister was rebuked in 1995 by Prime Minister John Major when he accused Princess Diana of being in the advanced stage of paranoia after she discussed the disintegration of her marriage to Charles on television.
LABOUR AVOIDING THE ISSUE

But Labour, a party with a strong vein of republicanism, has also avoided addressing the future of the monarchy as it became increasingly clear it was favourite to win the election. The subject is a political "no-go" zone, many Labour MPs complain.
During a five-hour setpiece debate on the constitution in February only one member of parliament touched upon the monarchy, veteran Labour left-winger Tony Benn.
"I am in favour of the Crown retiring with honour and a good pension to Buckingham Palace," said Benn, but he was careful to distance himself from criticism of the queen's family.
"The problem with the monarchy is about the Crown, not the royal family. The trouble is that Crown powers are enormous."

Benn's remarks highlighted his republican beliefs, which are shared by many Labour MPs -- about one quarter favour a republic, according to one poll. But to avoid rocking the boat, and revealing any splits within the party, they are keeping quiet.
The vexed subject was last addressed by Labour in March 1996 when Ron Davies, the party's spokesman for Wales, ran into trouble after questioning Charles's fitness to be king.
Blair immediately demanded an apology from Davies. But other senior members of Labour have not hidden their distaste for the power wielded by the 1,000-year monarchy.
DEBATE OVER ROLE OF THE MONARCHY
Jack Straw, Labour's home affairs spokesman, called in 1994 for a slimmed-down royal family that would have its political power reduced but would have the right to enter public debate.

Michael Meacher, one of only four Labour shadow cabinet members to have held a ministerial position, called in 1993 for an end to the mystique surrounding the royal family and the way "it is used to underpin a class system in this country".

Critics say it is absurd the queen still holds the power -- albeit rarely used -- to choose prime ministers. Labour does not believe in giving the vote to hereditary lords so why is it happy for hereditary monarchs to be head of state, they ask.
Blair himself, weeks before he became party leader, said he believed the monarchy could choose between "retreating into isolation or seeking to become more like a normal family".
But since his elevation to Labour's number one job, and the prospects of weekly meetings with the queen as prime minister grew, Blair has become more openly supportive.
In an interview marking the queen's 70th birthday in April 1996, Blair said he thought Charles was fit to be king and "the constitutional position of the monarchy is very clear".
"Everyone understands the problems the Royal Family has been through over the past few years but I don't think we should forget a lot of the good that is done," he told the BBC.

Blair believes the monarchy is making efforts to adapt and update its image with the queen's decision to pay income tax and her establishment of a "way forward" group to explore how the royal family could improve its public standing.

Neither major party addresses the monarchy in their election manifesto but a 1996 document containing Labour pledges states: "We have no plans to replace the monarchy". Commentators point out that it does not rule out some form of reform.
Blair hinted at possible reforms in April 1996. "I am a firm believer in the type of constitutional monarchy we have, but I also want to modernise our institutions," he said.
"Constitutional change is really about preserving what is best about our institutions and at the same time adapting them to the changing needs of our times."
Commentators say he may consider an all-party constitutional inquiry which could address the role of the monarchy.

"The new prime minister (if there is one) might do well to start off his constitutional agenda at the top, setting up a Royal Commission on the monarchy," said Ben Pimlott, author of a biography of the queen.
"The result might be the basis for a new settlement between Crown and people, soberly tailored for the needs of the new century."
